title: Four marks
hook: the church is one, holy, catholic and apostolic, each tradition explaining how

segments.voice: Yesterday, tongues, and three answers from one Bible. Your line was the spirit blows.

This Sunday, in a Catholic parish, an Orthodox cathedral and an Anglican chapel, people will stand and say the same old sentence from the Nicene Creed. It describes the church in four words: one, holy, catholic, apostolic. Then they'll go home to churches that are plainly not one, sometimes not holy, very local, and arguing about what the apostles meant. So what are they saying? A wish? A boast? A promise? These four words are the marks of the church: the signs you're meant to recognize it by. Day three hundred six met the small-c catholic. Today, all four.
screen: `A WISH, A BOAST, OR A PROMISE?`

segments.voice: One at a time. One. Paul writes to the Ephesians: "There is one body, and one Spirit, even as ye are called in one hope of your calling; One Lord, one faith, one baptism." And in John's Gospel Jesus prays "That they all may be one." Holy. Not because its members are spotless, but because it belongs to God, set apart. Catholic, small c: universal, for the whole, every place, every people, the whole faith. Apostolic. Paul says the household of God is "built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Jesus Christ himself being the chief corner stone." Now the explanations, side by side. The Catholic Church teaches that the one church of Christ subsists in the Catholic Church, apostolic through bishops in succession from the apostles, in communion with the pope, while recognizing real elements of the church beyond its walls. The Orthodox Church holds that it is the one church, kept apostolic by bishops who guard the faith handed down. Anglicans also keep bishops in succession and see themselves within the one catholic church. Protestant confessions like Augsburg find the church wherever the gospel is rightly preached and the sacraments rightly given; apostolic, for them, means teaching what the apostles taught. So the same words can describe a visible body with a shape and a history, or a fellowship of believers spread through many churches. One thing these explanations can share: the marks are said as faith, not as a report card. Christians say them on days when their own church looks nothing like them.
screen: `ONE BODY, ONE LORD, ONE BAPTISM.` · `HOLY: BELONGING TO GOD.` · `CATHOLIC: FOR THE WHOLE.` · `APOSTOLIC: BUILT ON THE APOSTLES.` · then, large: `ONE, HOLY, CATHOLIC, APOSTOLIC.`

segments.voice: If you belong to a church, bring it to mind, the building, the faces, the arguments, and run the four words past it: one, holy, catholic, apostolic, noticing which feels thinnest right now. If you pray, ask for that mark for your church by name. If you don't belong to a church, try the same with any community you're part of: a family, a team, a neighborhood.
Four marks. One, holy, catholic and apostolic: the signs of the church in the Nicene Creed, said together, explained differently.
Your line: one, holy, catholic, apostolic. Four old words, said together across churches. Day one thousand ninety-six.

howItsDone: Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican, Lutheran and other churches confess the church as one, holy, catholic and apostolic in the Nicene Creed, often aloud together at the Eucharist; each tradition explains the marks in its own way.

fork.setup: you say "one, holy, catholic, apostolic" on Sunday, but your church is split and struggling. what are you doing?
options: lying, so better to stop saying it.
confessing faith in what the church is in God's eyes and is called to be.
fork.reveal: the marks are said as faith, not a report card. traditions explain them differently, but none says them only on good days.

original.note: Greek: universal, for the whole — the word behind "catholic" in the creed.

what a scholar hears: the marks come from the Nicene Creed's line on the church; Lumen Gentium 8 and the Augsburg Confession, Article 7, explain them differently.

chat.says: Why do churches call themselves one, holy, catholic and apostolic when they're so divided?
options: The four marks are said as faith, not a report card, even when a church looks nothing like them.
Only one church says the Nicene Creed, so the other churches never use those words.
Holy here means every member is spotless, so the line is a boast about good behavior.
chat.meaning: The four marks come from the Nicene Creed, and churches explain them differently. They are said as faith, not a report card, even on hard days.

Nicene Creed.meaning: an ancient statement of faith said in many churches

apostolic.meaning: built on the apostles and what they taught

Augsburg.meaning: here, the Augsburg Confession, a Lutheran statement of faith

Anglicans.meaning: Christians of the Church of England and churches linked with it

notes: The phrase 'one, holy, catholic and apostolic' is a paraphrase of the creed's line; the BCP 1662 text omits 'holy' ('one Catholick and Apostolick Church'), so no translation is quoted.
Some free-church and Baptist congregations do not recite creeds; the hook says 'the churches that say them'.

Catholic summary paraphrases Lumen Gentium 8 ('subsists in') and its recognition of elements of sanctification and truth outside its visible structure. Orthodox, Anglican and Protestant (Augsburg VII) summaries: confirm fairness.
'Catholic ... means universal, for the whole' is a definitional gloss; the derivation from καθ' ὅλου appears in the trapdoor only. Confirm.
Hook's picture of Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican congregations saying the creed on Sunday: confirm phrasing.
